cards.h: A property with no everyday twin
cards.b:
Electrons have a built-in property called spin. It makes them tiny magnets, and it decides how atoms stack into the periodic table, how magnets work and how MRI scanners see inside the body.

The experiment that revealed its strangeness, in 1922, was done before anyone knew what spin was.

Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach in Frankfurt sent a beam of silver atoms through a magnetic field that is stronger on one side. A little compass-like atom is pushed up or down according to which way its magnet points.

If the atoms' tiny magnets pointed in random directions, you would expect a smear. Instead there were two clean spots. The magnetic direction is quantised: only two options.

Spin was named in 1925 by George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit, building on Wolfgang Pauli's "two-valuedness" of electrons (1924). Paul Dirac in 1928 showed it falls out of relativity. The electron has spin one-half: measured along any chosen direction, you find "up" or "down", never in-between.

Analogy breaks: it is not a ball spinning. An electron as a tiny ball would need to spin faster than light to produce this magnetism. Spin is an intrinsic quantum property.

Chain several Stern-Gerlach magnets. Pass only "up along z" atoms, then test sideways (x): 50-50 up or down. Now take the "x up" atoms and test z again: you again get 50-50 up/down, even though we had selected only "z up" before!

The sideways test erased the earlier information. Spin along z and along x cannot both be sharp, like position and momentum (see the uncertainty lesson). This is a clean example of superposition: "up along x" is an equal mix of "z up" and "z down".

Every particle has a fixed spin. Spin-half particles (electrons, protons, neutrons, quarks) are fermions. Particles with whole-number spin (photon: 1; Higgs: 0) are bosons. This difference rules whether particles can share a state (next lessons). A spin-half particle must be turned by two full circles (720°) to return to its starting state: an odd fact confirmed with neutrons in the 1970s.

• MRI. Hydrogen nuclei (protons) have spin. In a strong magnetic field they line up; radio pulses flip them and the signals map tissue (Lauterbur and Mansfield, Nobel 2003).
  • Hard drives and memory read magnetic spin (spintronics; Fert and Gruenberg, Nobel 2007).
  • Qubits. Spin up/down can be a quantum bit.

Stern-Gerlach with many atoms; fine splitting of spectral lines (Zeeman and fine-structure effects); electron-spin resonance; the structure of the periodic table. Stern received the 1943 Nobel for this work, and Rabi the 1944 Nobel for magnetic resonance of spins.

• "Spin means rotating." It behaves like angular momentum, but nothing spins.
  • "The up/down direction is built in before measuring." The sequential test shows it is not.
  • "Particles with spin-zero have no properties." They simply lack that magnetism.

Particles with whole-number spin are named bosons after S.N. Bose, the name coined by Paul Dirac. Bose's counting for photons (spin 1) applies to all of them. Nuclear magnetic resonance and MRI are widely used in India, and spin-based quantum devices are a research thrust in NQM hubs at IIT Bombay (sensing) and TIFR.

• Stern-Gerlach (1922): silver atoms split into two spots, so magnetic direction is quantised.
  • Spin is intrinsic, not a spinning ball.
  • Spin along different axes cannot both be sharp.

Think about it

  1. Why does a second test along z give 50-50 again after an x test?
  2. Why can an electron's spin not be due to a literally spinning ball?
